analysis.one_liner: Gives people legal rights to see, correct, delete, and limit companies' use of their online personal data, enforced by a new federal agency.
analysis.headline: The Online Privacy Act was introduced in November 2019, referred to two House committees and their subcommittees, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give internet users a set of enforceable rights over their personal data: the right to see what companies have on them, correct it, delete it, take it to a competitor, and get a human review of automated decisions about them. Companies would need clear consent to collect, sell, or use personal data for targeted personalization, could not use data to discriminate by race, sex, or other protected traits, and would have to notify people of breaches. A new United States Digital Privacy Agency, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, who today have little practical control over how companies collect, keep, and resell their personal information. The bill would let them access, correct, and delete their data, refuse behavioral profiling, learn exactly who a company sold their data to, and sue or complain to a new federal agency when companies mishandle it. It also would void pre-dispute arbitration agreements for privacy claims, so people could take violations to court.

how_it_helps.text: Gives individuals rights to access the personal information a company holds — including how it got it and which third parties it went to — and to correct or delete it, with answers due within 30 days and no fee for ordinary requests.

Requires express consent before a company collects risky personal data or uses an individual's information for behavioral personalization, and requires companies to offer a non-personalized version of the service when consent is refused.
Bars selling personal data unless the person consents to that specific sale and is told the identity of the buyer, and requires consent by category before disclosure to any third party.

Gives people the right to human review of consequential decisions made solely by automated processing, and bars processing data in ways that discriminate on the basis of race, sex, religion, disability, or other protected classes in jobs, credit, housing, insurance, and education.
Creates a United States Digital Privacy Agency with rulemaking, investigation, and litigation powers, and adds enforcement by state attorneys general, private lawsuits, and whistleblower protections.

Prohibits pre-dispute arbitration agreements for privacy claims, requires breach notification, restricts handling of genetic data and the contents of communications, and makes it a federal crime to publish someone's personal information with intent to intimidate or harass.
Requires data portability through real-time APIs for concentrated product categories, a mechanism aimed at letting users switch providers and increasing competition.

analysis.who_pays: Companies whose business models depend on collecting, profiling, and reselling personal information — data brokers, ad-tech firms, and large platforms built on targeted advertising. They would face consent requirements, data minimization duties, security mandates, and agency oversight. Consumers could face some indirect costs, such as compliance expenses passed through or the loss of some free, ad-supported personalized services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech, and large platforms

drawbacks.text: Extensive carve-outs: businesses under $25 million in revenue with under 200 employees are exempt from most duties, and data that is de-identified or handled with 'privacy preserving computing' can be processed without consent, which some privacy advocates argue leaves large channels open.

Companies may deny a product or service entirely if behavioral personalization is infeasible to remove, so in limited cases users could face a consent-or-lose-service choice rather than a true opt-out.

Enforcement depends on funding a brand-new federal agency through annual appropriations, so the strength of protections would hinge on future Congresses resourcing it, though state enforcement and private suits provide backups.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For everyday internet users the bill's protections — access, deletion, sale transparency, anti-discrimination limits, and a ban on forced arbitration for privacy claims — outweigh the costs, which fall mainly on the data-driven businesses whose practices create the risks. The honest cost side is real: compliance would burden smaller firms (which the bill largely exempts), some personalized free services could be scaled back, and the new agency would need steady funding. Design choices like the de-identified-data carve-outs are debatable, but the bill's core trade — user control over data in exchange for compliance costs on the data industry — clearly favors the public.

outcome.mechanism: It went to two House committees and their subcommittees in late 2019, neither took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended without ever reaching a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the Online Privacy Act of 2019 on November 5, 2019, joined by Rep. Zoe Lofgren.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Judiciary Committee — a dual referral that requires two committees to act before the bill can advance.

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce on November 6, 2019, and to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law on December 18, 2019.
The bill attracted 4 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action of any kind is recorded after the December 2019 subcommittee referral.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, digital advertisers, and large platforms that profile users came out ahead: with no law enacted, they kept the ability to collect, process, and sell Americans' personal information with no federal consent regime, breach rules beyond existing patchwork law, or dedicated privacy regulator.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Democratic — Eshoo, Lofgren, and 4 Democratic cosponsors, with no Republicans — but the bill never reached a committee or floor vote, so no vote ever recorded a party split.

industries.note: The bill would bar selling personal data without per-sale consent and disclosure of the buyer's identity, ending the practice of quietly trading people's information. Data brokers' revenue depends on the opposite, so their interest runs directly against the people the bill protects.

The bill requires consent for cross-context advertising identifiers and bars disclosures for ad targeting that would let one disclosure be linked to another, cutting into the profiling that underpins ad-tech revenue. Ordinary users would gain control over the same data flows.

Platforms built on behavioral personalization would have to get express consent, offer non-personalized versions of their services, minimize collection, and answer to a new regulator — a direct cost to their dominant business model. The portability requirements also aim to make it easier for users to leave them.

Firms under $25 million in revenue with fewer than 200 employees are exempt from most of the bill's duties and get a nine-month ramp when they outgrow the exemption, sparing them most compliance costs.
